file-size-converter.quickAnswer: 2.5 GB = 2,500 MB in decimal math (×1,000) or 2,560 MiB in binary math (×1,024). Pick Decimal for how storage makers and the web measure files, Binary for how operating systems see them. Enter a value, choose from/to units, and swap any time.
keyFacts: Decimal (SI): each step ×1,000. 1 MB = 1,000 KB = 1,000,000 bytes.
Binary (IEC): each step ×1,024. 1 MiB = 1,024 KiB = 1,048,576 bytes.
The two systems differ by 2.4% at KB, 4.9% at MB and 7.4% at GB - enough to matter for upload limits.
A "100 MB upload limit" is usually decimal: 100,000,000 bytes.
Email attachments are often capped around 25 MB - compress or split bigger files.
Video bitrate math: a 10 Mbps stream for 60 s ≈ 75 MB (10 ÷ 8 × 60).
howTo: Pick the from-unit and to-unit (B, KB, MB, GB, TB).
Read the instant result; swap reverses it.
file-size-converter.formula:
result = value × (bytes per from-unit) ÷ (bytes per to-unit).
Decimal: KB 1,000, MB 10⁶, GB 10⁹, TB 10¹².
Binary: KB 1,024, MB 1,048,576, GB 1,073,741,824, TB 1,099,511,627,776.
Example (decimal): 2.5 GB → MB = 2.5 × 10⁹ ÷ 10⁶ = 2,500 MB.
benefits: Both math systems in one tool - match whatever your platform actually uses.
Settles upload-limit questions: is that 100 MB decimal or binary?
Handy for video, backup and attachment size planning.
limitations: Converts the number only - actual files carry filesystem overhead that changes on-disk size.
Upload limits on real sites may use either system; check the site docs when it matters.
Does not estimate compression; zipping changes the real byte count.

faqs.q: How many KB are in 1 MB?
faqs.a: 1,000 KB in decimal math, 1,024 KiB in binary math. File managers and web upload limits almost always mean decimal; RAM and OS internals mean binary.

faqs.q: How many MB are in 1 GB?
faqs.a: 1,000 MB decimal or 1,024 MiB binary. A "16 GB" phone has about 16,000 MB of decimal storage before the OS and formatting take their share.

faqs.q: Should I use decimal or binary?
faqs.a: Use decimal (×1,000) when talking about files, downloads, and storage products - that is what makers and the web use. Use binary (×1,024) for memory, OS internals, and developer tooling.

faqs.q: Why is my 1 TB drive only 931 GB?
faqs.a: The maker counts decimal terabytes (10¹² bytes). Your OS divides by 1,024³, showing 931 GiB. Same bytes, different ruler - try the Byte Size Calculator to see both.

faqs.q: How big can an email attachment be?
faqs.a: Most providers cap attachments around 25 MB (decimal). For bigger files, use a cloud link instead of attaching.

faqs.q: How do I estimate video file size?
faqs.a: Size ≈ bitrate × seconds ÷ 8. A 10 Mbps video for 60 seconds ≈ 10 ÷ 8 × 60 = 75 MB. Add ~5% for container overhead.

mistakes: Converting on the wrong tab — a '100 MB upload limit' is almost always decimal. Using binary math tells you 104.86 MB and you under-fill for nothing.
Converting MB→KB then reading the answer as KB→MB: direction errors give 1,000,000× wrong answers. Always glance at From/To.
Forgetting that 'MB' on the site and 'MiB' in your OS are different units — a 700 MB file can show as 667 MiB after download and nothing is lost.
Treating the number as the final file size — filesystems, zips and email encoding change the real byte count. Convert, then add headroom.
Rounding mid-chain: converting GB→MB→KB with rounded intermediates drifts. Convert directly from the original value instead.
